title: MITOMYCIN-C (MMC): The Ophthalmic Double-Edged Sword
summary: Mitomycin-C is a potent DNA-crosslinking alkylating agent isolated from Streptomyces caespitosus. Used as a powerful modulator of wound healing, it is indispensable in glaucoma filtration, refractive surgery, and ocular oncology, requiring precise dosing and handling due to its significant cytotoxic potential.

sections.title: Definition & Pharmacological Overview
sections.content: Mitomycin-C (MMC) is a potent antineoplastic antibiotic derived from Streptomyces caespitosus. It functions as a prodrug that undergoes bioreductive activation to become a multi-functional alkylating agent. In ophthalmology, it is primarily used off-label (except for Mitosol) to inhibit fibroblast proliferation and reduce scarring by preventing DNA replication, mitosis, and protein synthesis.

sections.title: Mechanism of Action: The Alkylation Cascade
Clinical Applications in Ophthalmology
content: Glaucoma Filtration Surgery: Applied to the subconjunctival space/scleral flap to prevent bleb failure in Trabeculectomy and GDD surgery.
Refractive Surgery: Prophylactic use in PRK, LASEK, and PTK to prevent post-operative subepithelial haze (especially in high myopia or deep ablations).
Ocular Surface Oncology: Primary or adjuvant treatment for OSSN (Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia) and Primary Acquired Melanosis (PAM) with atypia.
Pterygium Surgery: Intraoperative application to the bare sclera or postoperative drops to reduce recurrence rates.
Cicatrizing Disease: Used in symblepharon lysis and DCR surgery to maintain ostium patency.
Corneal Procedures: Treatment of recurrent Salzmann's nodular degeneration or band keratopathy.

sections.title: Contraindications & Extreme Cautions
content: Active Ocular Infection
Pregnancy or Breastfeeding (Category X)
Pre-existing Scleral Thinning or Necrosis
Severe Dry Eye or Neurotrophic Keratopathy
Hypersensitivity to Mitomycin-C
Sjogren's Syndrome (high risk of melt)

sections.title: Intraoperative Application Process (Trabeculectomy)
content: Step 1: Reconstitution of MMC powder with sterile water or BSS (e.g., Mitosol kit).
Step 2: Dissection of Conjunctival Peritomy (usually limbus-based or fornix-based).
Step 3: Placement of MMC-soaked sponges (number and size vary) under Tenon's capsule.
Step 4: Ensure edges of conjunctiva are not in contact with MMC to avoid wound leak.
Step 5: Timer initiation for the specific duration (1-5 mins based on risk factors).
Step 6: Removal of all sponges and meticulous counting.
Step 7: Copious irrigation with 20-30mL of BSS to neutralize/remove residual MMC.

sections.title: MMC Preparation & Safety (NIOSH Guidelines)
content: Must be prepared in a Class II Biological Safety Cabinet (Laminar Flow).
Double-gloving and protective gowns required for staff.
Use of Luer-lock syringes to prevent accidental spray.
Chemotherapy-grade disposal containers for all sponges and sharps.
Avoid skin contact; if contact occurs, wash with soap and water immediately.

sections.title: Memory Aid: The 4 'C's of MMC Toxicity

content.explanation: C - Conjunctival thinning/avascularity; C - Cornea (melt and PED); C - Calcification of the sclera; C - Cataract (secondary to metabolic shift).

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The Evidence Base
content: Fluorouracil Filtering Surgery Study (FFSS): Established antimetabolites in glaucoma, but highlighted the superiority of MMC in high-risk cases.
Chen et al. (1990): Pioneered the use of MMC in trabeculectomy, showing significant IOP reduction compared to 5-FU.
The Mitosol Trial: Phase 3 study leading to FDA approval of the first standardized MMC kit for ophthalmic surgery.
Majmudar et al. (2000): Established the 0.02% protocol for haze prevention in PRK.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Always count sponges: A retained MMC sponge is a surgical catastrophe.
Bleb Management: MMC blebs are typically thin, cystic, and avascular; watch for late-onset leaks.
Topical OSSN Use: Instruct patients to use punctal occlusion and chilled drops to reduce irritation.
Reconstitution: MMC is unstable in solution; use within 24 hours (unless commercially stabilized like Mitosol).

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
sections.content: In pediatric glaucoma, wound healing is exceptionally aggressive. MMC is often used in primary trabeculectomies in children, but with shorter exposure times (2 mins) and lower concentrations (0.2 mg/mL) to minimize the lifelong risk of thin-walled bleb endophthalmitis, which is higher in the pediatric population.
